title.analysis: Authentic title "How Everything Changes After Your Investments Beat Your Salary" uses a threshold/transformation frame (the investment-income crossover) with second-person address. It is structurally close to the STRONG peer "Why Everything Changes After You Hit $1,000,000 Invested" (same "Everything Changes After" construction) but replaces a dollar threshold with a relative one. The script delivers the crossover via 7% return multiples, a two-coworker contrast and savings-rate arithmetic. TYPICAL against the cohort; association only, no CTR or experiment evidence.

script.opening_words: You're sitting in your car in the work parking lot, not because you forgot something, because you opened your banking app while the engine was still running. It's just a quick check, 30 seconds, and now you need a moment before you go in. The number is fine, it's always fine, it's just never quite as fine as you'd like, and you can't entirely explain why, because by every reasonable measure, you're doing okay. Good job, decent salary, you got
script.ending_words: bigger than their paycheck. That's the crossover and it doesn't happen to lucky people. It happens to people who treated a $5,000 raise like it didn't exist, opened a brokerage app instead of an apartment listing, and then waited long enough for the math to catch up. You can't rush compound interest, but you absolutely can start it. And starting it today is worth more than starting it perfectly tomorrow.
script.analysis: Full 20929 canonical characters read. A crossover explainer: two-coworker cold open, 4% rule and 25x targets, return multiples at 7%, a $1,000/month compounding timeline, a $78,000 earner budget, savings-rate years to FI, teacher vs surgeon, lifestyle creep and car payments, the coworker's portfolio crossing milestones, tax treatment of earned vs investment income, what FI people actually do (T. Rowe Price), money and control, national savings data, three levers (start now, savings rate, avoid creep), the Ramsey millionaire study, and a close. Reproduced: 25x targets, $521K/$1.22M compounding, the $3,911 budget, teacher/surgeon targets, $500/month 25-vs-35 gap, median 401(k) yield. Slightly off: final-decade growth $699K not $680K; crossover 41 not 43 years. Overstated: federal tax on $100K MFJ wages is about $7,640 (2026), not $11,500, and the marginal rate is 12%, not 22%. Stale: 0% LTCG threshold $94,000 is 2024; 2026 is $98,900. Supported: Ramsey study figures. Unverified: T. Rowe 57%, 74% control, 40% emergency, 4.9% savings rate. The "$70,000 per year" from $1M at 7% conflicts with the video's own 4% rule. One ASR omission ("you need million"). The stored ending is complete.

claim_audit.assessment: IRS2026: 2026 MFJ standard deduction $32,200; 0% LTCG bracket to $98,900 taxable income. K02: $100,000 wages - $32,200 = $67,800 taxable; tax = 10% x 24,800 + 12% x 43,000 = $7,640, not $11,500 (overstated by ~50%). $94,000 is the 2024 threshold (stale). Zero tax on $100,000 of qualified income holds ($67,800 taxable < $98,900).

topic.audience_problem: Salaried workers doing "fine" who see no path from paycheck income to financial independence.
topic.time_sensitivity: Low-medium: evergreen mechanism, but tax thresholds date annually.
topic.narrative_angle: Two identical coworkers diverge because one let the math run.
